How to Read This Chart
The bar spans developer spending. Min spend is the least the entered package's mix must cost to return the break-even floor in public value; it moves with the package's value ratio. Package budget, low is the conservative value to developer less the modeled fees paid at building permit, which is why it sits below the value-to-developer figure; package budget, high is the same on the low build-cost end. The marker is the estimated developer cost of the entered package, and the shaded band is the fair-share reference.
Pool Scarcity
Whether this request draws from a density pool and, where it does, how the pool balance feeds the break-even floor. The pool chart is on Step 1; allocations are in the Allocation Ledger.
Fiscal Impacts (Fiscal Snapshot & Counterfactual)
Property-tax context by level of government. Context only, never part of the decision.
Sensitivity: Robustness (±20% Sketch)
Moves each model figure 20% the wrong way at once and reports whether the decision survives. Developer value is stressed from the conservative (low) estimate, the same basis the developer-value budget test uses; the modeled fees stay fixed.
Sensitivity: Deal Explorer (What-If Spend)
Drag to test a larger or smaller package of the same mix. What-if only; does not change the entered package.
Tampa Comparison (10:1 / ICC Construction-Cost Basis)
An optional cross-check against the basis SPB Planning cited (Tampa Code 27-140 and ICC). It compares the developer’s benefit spend to the bonus units' construction cost at the ICC R-2 (residential, multiple family) rate, so it is shown for condominium and multifamily rental projects and withheld for temporary lodging. Reference only, not part of the decision. Inputs editable under Assumptions § F.
Benefits Ranked by Priority-Weighted Value
Public value per developer dollar, times the category priority weight (the multiplier in parentheses, set in Assumptions § D). Ranking only: the weights do not change credited public value or the verdict.

User Guide

Estimate bonus-density value, compare public benefits, and test negotiation scenarios.

This tool supports staff analysis of density and density-pool requests. It does not establish project approval, legal authority for an exaction, nexus or proportionality, or a required contribution.

1Define the Project

Enter the project location, use, site area, verified baseline entitlement and proposed development. Confirm the applicable density pathway and resolve any warnings before relying on the result.

2Build the Benefit Package

Add public benefits proposed in connection with the request. Include only benefits above existing requirements and review both estimated developer cost and credited public value.

3Review the Result

The tool asks two primary questions:

  • Does the proposed package meet the modeled public-value floor?
  • Is its estimated developer cost within the modeled developer-value budget?

Supporting context helps staff interpret the result.

4Apply Staff Judgment

Use the modeled result alongside applicable code requirements, project impacts, planning objectives, benefit deliverability and legal review. The tool informs the discretionary decision; it does not replace it.

When a result is withheld. The tool will withhold a definitive result when required project, entitlement, density-pathway or pool information has not been confirmed. Resolve the displayed warning before relying on the conclusion.

Reading the Results page. Decision shows whether the package clears the modeled public-value floor and whether the estimated developer cost fits within the modeled developer-value budget. Context provides supporting information such as pool scarcity, fiscal effects, fair-share references, comparison benchmarks and sensitivity testing. Technical Details show the underlying assumptions and calculations.

Need more detail? Open the calculation pages or the technical and legal reference sections below.

Technical and Legal Reference

District & Pool Coverage

What the Tool Models

The tool models the main residential and temporary-lodging pools and a separate Large Resort pathway.

This tool prices pool scarcity for two finite pools: the 195-unit residential pool (LDC §39.18) and the 325-unit transient-lodging pool shared by the Town Center Corey Circle / Coquina West, Activity Center and Bayou Residential districts (Future Land Use element).

These are not the only sources of added units: Large Resort adds lodging by conditional use within its district maximum, with no pool draw, and the city's other lodging pools (Town Center Core 50, Boutique Hotel/Condo 125, Upham Beach Village 175) are not modeled by this tool, so no pool value or public-value floor is established for a request that draws on one of them.

Each pool allocation is by Commission ordinance plus conditional use on a "merit basis" (LDC §4.12(d)), whose benefit menu (1)–(9) maps to the categories here.

The Comprehensive Plan's residential unit reserves for Downtown Core Residential (23 units) and the two Commercial Corridor districts (22 and 64) are not modeled by this tool either.

For pool allocations, the modeled ledger balance comes from the Allocation Ledger. The projected demand for each pool and the planning horizon come from Assumptions. Pool balances reflect the tool's ledger, not a live city allocation register. Confirm balances, district limits and approval requirements against current records.

Residential Pool and Town Center Districts

Residential pool requests are checked against pool availability only (LDC Sec. 39.18(d) sets no project, acreage or district cap); awards remain at the City Commission's discretion and development standards still apply.

A use from the other unit class than a district is modeled for (a condominium in Large Resort or Gulf Boulevard, lodging in a Town Center or residential district) is reported as "Not modeled by this tool", and no verdict is issued for it. That status describes the tool's coverage, not the use's eligibility: whether the district's own provisions provide a pathway is a question for Planning.

Large Resort

Large Resort calculations exclude pool scarcity; the tool selects the Large Resort scale tier on gross site acreage, following the Comprehensive Plan (a parcel of at least three gross acres); LDC Sec. 35.2 says "buildable site", so that basis is pending planner confirmation and a request that fits the cap under only one reading gets no overall conclusion.

Gulf Boulevard: Activity Center, Bayou Residential, Boutique Hotel/Condo

In the Gulf Boulevard group the lodging rules follow the character district, read from the embedded City land-use layer or set by staff on Step 1. A pin or parcel inside one of the three sets it, and staff can set or change it in the character district list on Step 1. While the character district is not established, no lodging cap, per-project limit or pool is applied and no verdict is issued.

  • Activity Center: up to 40 TLU/ac and 50 units per project from the shared 325-unit pool, on a buildable site of at least one acre, and to qualify for mixed-use densities at least 10 temporary lodging units mixed with at least 0.35 FAR of commercial or office use, which staff confirm on Step 1 (the tool does not model the mixed-use program). On the Activity Center lodging pathway, tick Staff confirmed AC mixed-use eligibility once the mixed-use standards are confirmed; until then the result stays conditional. The tool does not determine the buildable site: where the density-eligible area entered is below one acre, also tick Staff confirmed minimum one-acre buildable-site requirement once that is confirmed. The tool screens on the density-eligible area; until that and the mixed-use standard are confirmed, the result stays conditional.
  • Bayou Residential: up to 40 TLU/ac, subject to available units in the applicable shared lodging pool. The Bayou Residential provisions state no per-project figure (LDC Sec. 42.6(d)) and the tool applies none; confirm with Planning whether a per-project allocation limit applies.
  • Boutique Hotel/Condo: 50 TLU/ac (a conditional use above 30), plus up to 20/ac and 60 units per project from its own 125-unit pool. A request within the 50 TLU/ac draws no pool units and is evaluated without a pool. The tool does not model that pool's balance, so for a request that needs pool units it shows the density rules but no pool balance, pool value or public-value floor, and issues no verdict.

Outside the Redevelopment District

For the two entries outside the redevelopment district, the applicable density limit is not established by the selection, so the entered by-right is the baseline.

When a Result Is Withheld or Conditional

Decision order: coverage limits and missing inputs come first. Each of the following withholds the overall conclusion whatever the package shows:

  • a use that this tool does not model in the selected district ("Not modeled by this tool");
  • a Gulf Boulevard lodging request whose character district is not established ("Gulf Boulevard character district not established");
  • a Boutique Hotel/Condo lodging request that needs units from its separate 125-unit pool, whose balance is not modeled ("Boutique Hotel/Condo pool balance not modeled");
  • a blank by-right entitlement ("By-right baseline not established");
  • a blank or unconfirmed impact contribution.

In the two Gulf Boulevard states the shared 325-unit lodging pool is not applied, so no pool balance, scarcity value or public-value floor is shown, and the developer estimates remain for reference only. A Boutique Hotel/Condo request within the 50 TLU/ac available without a pool draw needs no pool units and is evaluated normally, with no pool value.

An open density basis also withholds the overall conclusion:

  • no district selected ("District not set");
  • a density-eligible area larger than the total site area ("Density-eligible area exceeds the total site area");
  • no density-eligible site area where the district has a density cap ("Site area not entered");
  • a Large Resort request that fits the cap under only one of the two acreage readings ("Density tier requires confirmation");
  • a requested lodging total above the district cap ("Request exceeds district cap");
  • a pool request above the modeled ledger balance ("Request exceeds remaining pool") or above the Activity Center limit of 50 units per project ("Request exceeds per-project pool cap");
  • an Activity Center lodging request whose density-eligible area is below one acre and whose one-acre buildable-site requirement staff have not confirmed ("Activity Center buildable-site requirement requires confirmation"), or one whose mixed-use eligibility staff have not confirmed ("Activity Center pathway eligibility not fully established").

In those cases the financial results stay visible and are labeled conditional; they do not indicate that the request can be granted. While a Large Resort by-right is waiting on the site area, the figures that depend on the bonus request are withheld instead. When the acreage is in error, the stress test and the Deal Explorer are also marked not assessed.

The entered package's own two tests come next, so an offer that meets the floor within the budget passes even when the floor exceeds the budget; the status says exactly what was met ("Meets the break-even floor; below the fair-share reference band"), and only a package that also reaches the fair-share reference band is shown in green.

"Hold" and "No zone" appear when the package fails its tests, or before any benefits are entered when the floor already exceeds the whole budget; because the floor is public value and the budget is developer spending, they state the value-to-cost rate a package would need in order to clear.

Mapping & Site Data

How the District Is Detected

Enter the project name and location. Confirm the district, use and approval pathway, then select parcels or enter site area manually.

An exact City district code on the embedded land-use layer sets the district automatically. Where that layer has no answer, a countywide layer is asked; a general category there (for example "Activity Center" or "Town Center") does not identify a City district, so the pin line reads "District requires confirmation", a district that staff selected is kept, a district read from a map layer at an earlier pin is reset to Unknown, and staff confirm the district.

Site Area and Density-Eligible Area

Review Density-Eligible Area separately from total site area. The tool uses eligible area for density calculations and gross area for fiscal comparisons (in Large Resort, the tool also uses gross area to select the scale tier; that basis is pending planner confirmation). Map-derived values require verification. The eligible area cannot exceed the total site area: when it does, Step 1 shows an error and no density check or overall conclusion is issued until one of the two figures is corrected.

Density is counted on the area landward of the CCCL.

Method Basis

Project Inputs the Method Relies On

  • By-right baseline. Set the by-right entitlement and the total proposed units or hotel rooms (the bonus request is total minus by-right; the slider also edits it directly). A blank by-right entitlement is not read as zero. Unless the tool derives it (Large Resort), the bonus request and the figures that depend on it are withheld until a verified baseline is entered; typing 0 records a zero baseline.
  • Cost and market value. Then enter the hard construction cost and the market value per unit or key, or use the estimators; enter hard cost only, since soft costs, developer margin and condominium sales cost are added on top. The construction benchmark scales with the entered average unit size from the hard-cost row's reference basis in Assumptions section A (defaults: 2,269 SF condo/MF, 750 SF per key).
  • Bonus-unit impact contribution. A blank field counts as not reviewed and withholds the verdict, typing 0 records a reviewed zero, and a figure entered for one use type must be reconfirmed if the use type changes.

Core Calculations

  • Value to developer: the estimated incremental value created by the bonus units.
  • Break-even floor: the modeled public-value threshold associated with the requested allocation.
  • Public value offered: the credited value of the entered benefit package.

Review each calculation page for the full derivation.

Value to developer is estimated as a range that reflects construction-cost uncertainty. Direct construction-cost overrides are tested at 15% above and below the entered amount. The value-decline factor applied to value to developer is a uniform adjustment, not cash-flow discounting.

The two package tests check whether public value offered is at or above the break-even floor, and whether estimated developer cost is at or below the available package budget. Meeting the floor is a modeled comparison, not a finding that the allocation is warranted. Fitting the budget is not a finding of project feasibility: the tool is not a full development pro forma.

Benefit Valuation

Add benefits from the Benefit Library. Enter only quantities above existing requirements. You can edit totals or per-unit values. Changing quantity recalculates both totals (estimated developer cost and public value). Record supporting information under Notes & Source.

How estimated developer cost, public value and the value ratio are defined, and how benefits are credited, is set out on the public value offered page under Valuation Notes.

Negotiation Range and Fair-Share Reference

The ZOPA chart converts the public-value floor into developer spending using the current package's value ratio. Its fair-share band is an editable policy assumption (Assumptions section F), not an adopted requirement. An offer below that band can still pass both package tests.

What code does not set. For the public-benefit package, no contribution rate, benefit-valuation formula, floor, or ceiling. LDC Sec. 29.12 separately sets a proportionate fair-share formula for transportation concurrency mitigation, which is not modeled by this tool. The tool does not perform a Chapter 163 proportionate-share calculation; the bonus-unit impact contribution is an entered figure pending a study.

The ZOPA bounds and the fair-share band (25 to 50% of the available package budget by default) are the TBRPC framework's judgment bands, not rates adopted in code or drawn from a specific study. The floor adds that entered contribution to a modeled pool value. Neither establishes what the city can require, which is a legal question (Chapter 163 proportionate-share; Nollan / Dolan / Koontz) for the City Attorney.

The ceiling reflects the general land-value-capture principle that a jurisdiction can share in part of the density-driven land-value uplift rather than all of it. Treat both as editable starting points to calibrate against local practice, not empirical constants.

Modeled Fees

The modeled fees are the Pinellas multimodal impact fee and, for residential uses, the City parks/rec impact fee; wastewater connection and other charges are not included unless entered, and credits or redevelopment adjustments can change the fees actually due. They are itemized under Assumptions § E.

Other Results Tools

  • Package Gap: Three figures: the public-value shortfall against the floor, the developer budget remaining after the estimated developer cost (or the amount over budget), and that cost as a share of the available package budget against the fair-share band, which is a policy reference and not an adopted requirement. The shortfall is public value and the budget is developer spending, so they are not interchangeable dollar for dollar. None of the three is evaluated for a use that is not modeled by this tool in the selected district, while the Gulf Boulevard character district is not established, or for a Boutique Hotel/Condo lodging request that needs pool units (that pool's balance is not modeled). Choosing benefits to close a gap depends on site conditions, community priorities, ownership and deliverability, so the tool does not generate a package.
  • Benefit Ranking: Applies category priority weights to value ratios. Weights affect ranking, not credited public value or the two package tests.
  • Deal Explorer: Tests spending at a fixed value ratio without changing the entered package.
  • Robustness: Applies simultaneous 20% adverse changes to the model estimates. Developer value is stressed from the conservative (low) estimate, the same basis the developer-value budget test uses; the modeled fees remain fixed.
  • Fiscal Snapshot and Tampa/ICC Cross-Check: Reference calculations that do not determine the verdict. The Fiscal Snapshot's city figure is property-tax revenue less modeled service cost (an annual cost per unit or key from Assumptions section K); other city revenues and costs are not modeled. It withholds the bonus versus by-right comparison while the by-right baseline is not established (a blank by-right entitlement, no district selected, a use this tool does not model in the district, or a Gulf Boulevard character district that is not established). The cross-check uses the ICC R-2 (residential, multiple family) rate and is withheld for temporary lodging, which is ICC Group R-1.

Results Page Layout

The Results page has four parts. Decision shows one status heading and a short sentence, with eligibility flags, a $0 floor and the legal qualifier visible beneath it. Core Numbers holds the four figures and the package gap. Context holds reference views (negotiation range, pool scarcity, fiscal impacts, sensitivity, the Tampa comparison and the benefit ranking); nothing opened or adjusted there changes the decision. Technical Details holds the formulas and the fee reconciliation under Calculation Details, the draft memo, and links to the assumptions and method.

The printed summary carries the Decision, the Core Numbers and the Calculation Details in full; it does not reproduce every Context view (the Tampa comparison, the benefit ranking and the Deal Explorer are on screen only).

Model Limitations

Results depend on entered assumptions. The model omits a full development cash flow and holds land cost constant. Added density may create costs across the entire project that a per-bonus-unit estimate misses. Scarcity curves, impact contributions, the fair-share reference band and unsupported cost inputs remain assumptions.

Legal Guardrails

This tool is advisory. It does not determine legal authority, nexus, rough proportionality, exaction validity, project approval or a legally required contribution. Applicable Charter, Code, Comprehensive Plan, state law and City Attorney guidance control.

Surfaced as caveats, not enforced in the math. Route the exaction framing through the City Attorney before treating any number as actionable.

  • Charter history. The 2006 citizen-initiated charter amendments requiring voter approval of comprehensive plan amendments, community redevelopment plans, and height increases were repealed by referendum in March 2011; related litigation over the comprehensive plan continued for years after. This tool assumes no charter referendum trigger applies to pool allocations within the adopted plan. Confirm the current charter with the City Attorney before relying on this assumption, and before pursuing anything that requires a plan amendment.
  • Live Local Act. Section 166.04151, Florida Statutes, may establish development rights independent of the City's local bonus-density process for qualifying affordable multifamily projects, including statutory standards affecting land use, density, floor area ratio, and height. Those rights may materially affect the project's development baseline and negotiating position. Applicability should be independently verified before relying on this tool's bonus-density analysis.
  • Exactions doctrine (Nollan / Dolan / Koontz / Sheetz). Any required benefit must satisfy essential nexus and rough proportionality, extended to monetary exactions by Koontz (2013) and to legislative fee schedules by Sheetz (2024). Exposure is highest when a benefit is priced off land-value uplift rather than impacts. The tool does not test either requirement: the pool-value part of its floor is priced from the developer's residual value, the impact part is an entered figure, and neither comes from a nexus or proportionality study.
  • State offset rule §166.04151. If the city ever mandates affordable units, it must fully offset the developer's cost. Voluntary bonus density is a different posture, but a mandate changes the math.

Confirm benefit eligibility, delivery terms, fee credits and any required mitigation separately. The tool's dollar thresholds do not establish legal authority, nexus, proportionality or project approval.

Not legal advice. Confirm density / FAR figures and pool balances against the adopted Comprehensive Plan and the live Municode LDC.

Saved Work & Settings

Settings

Use Enable editing to change Assumptions, Benefit Library values or the Allocation Ledger. Applied assumptions generally use the midpoint of low and high values unless overridden.

Saved Scenarios

Save scenario stores a snapshot for comparison. On a hosted page, scenarios are saved in this browser's storage, which can be cleared at any time and is not shared between machines; opened as a local file, they are held in memory and clear on reload. Export scenarios as JSON for backup or transfer: the exported .json file is the durable copy.

Loading an older scenario recalculates it under the current tool version. An older scenario saved with a by-right of 0 loads with the baseline not established; type 0 to confirm a zero baseline.

A Gulf Boulevard lodging scenario saved under an earlier version is listed as "Saved under an earlier version; load to re-evaluate": its stored decision predates the character-district rules. After loading it, confirm the character district on Step 1 and, for Activity Center, the mixed-use eligibility and, where the density-eligible area is below one acre, the buildable-site requirement.

A scenario priced on the residential pool or the shared temporary-lodging pool and saved before each pool had its own projected-demand assumption is listed the same way: its stored result used one shared demand figure. Loading it applies the default assumption for each pool; the shared figure is not carried over.

Reset All clears the project and benefits while retaining assumptions and the allocation ledger. Test Project loads a reference example and replaces the current project and benefits.

Memo and Print

Draft Staff Memo and Print/PDF: Summarize the decision, the figures behind it and the caveats. The Tampa comparison, the benefit ranking and the Deal Explorer are on screen only. The memo opens from "Draft Staff Memo" under Technical Details. Review before use.

Ledger

Allocation Ledger

Conditional-use approvals that drew from a density pool. Approved allocations from the two modeled pools (195 RU, 325 TLU) reduce the modeled ledger balance and drive the scarcity cost on Results; rows marked Other pool are recorded but not counted. Add a row per decision.

Save snapshots of inputs and results to compare side by side. Figures are frozen at save time under the version shown per row. Loading replaces the current inputs and re-evaluates under today's methodology, so an older snapshot may read differently.

Comparable Programs

How other jurisdictions connect additional development capacity to public benefits, and what those approaches can offer St. Pete Beach. Reference only. These examples do not feed the tool's calculations.

For this comparison, programs are grouped into three broad approaches. Some award additional density through a formula; others link development capacity to a menu of public benefits or manage growth through allocation limits. Their mechanisms offer useful reference points, but each operates under different legal requirements, development conditions and community priorities.

ApproachExamplesHow It WorksRelevance to St. Pete Beach
Formula-Based IncentivesTampa's bonus-cost ratio; Sarasota's attainable-housing density multipliers; California's State Density Bonus LawAdditional density or floor area is calculated from qualifying contributions, affordable-housing percentages or prescribed multipliers.Provides examples of transparent exchanges between development capacity and public benefits. Adapting a formula would require consideration of SPB's allocation criteria and limited pool availability.
Public-Benefit ProgramsClearwater's public-amenity incentives; Austin's Downtown Density Bonus Program; Montgomery County's incentive zoningAdditional development capacity is linked to specified benefits, contributions or evaluation criteria.Offers ways to define eligible benefits, document commitments and compare proposals consistently. Benefits and requirements would need to reflect SPB's priorities.
Growth Controls and Allocation SystemsMonroe County's ROGO; Key West's BPAS; Longboat Key's density referendumsDevelopment is constrained through permit allocations or voter approval requirements.Provides context for managing limited development capacity. These mechanisms do not, by themselves, establish the economic value or appropriate public-benefit contribution for an SPB allocation.

How St. Pete Beach Differs

St. Pete Beach's adopted framework includes a pool of 195 residential units and a pool of 325 temporary-lodging units, the two pools this tool models. It also includes other lodging pools (for example a 50-unit Town Center Core pool and a 125-unit Boutique Hotel-Condo pool), which are not modeled by this tool, and a Large Resort pathway that adds lodging by conditional use within the district cap, with no pool draw. The pool figures describe established pool capacity, not the current unallocated balance. Availability must be confirmed against city records, including prior awards and any units returned to a pool.

The residential reserve allows discretionary awards by the City Commission under adopted criteria. Temporary-lodging allocations are subject to their applicable district provisions. Allocation requirements therefore need to be checked for the specific project and pool.

The programs above can inform how SPB defines, evaluates and documents public benefits. Applying their rates or requirements locally would require additional analysis of the city's adopted framework and project conditions.

Selected Mechanisms
  • Tampa, Florida: The code establishes a 10:1 bonus-cost ratio for qualifying improvements outside the Channel District. Each $1 contributed translates into $10 in equivalent development dollars, which are converted into bonus units or floor area using development costs. Other provisions use different ratios.
  • Sarasota, Florida: Eligible downtown projects may achieve up to four times base density; eligible commercial corridor and center projects may achieve up to three times base density. At least 15% of the units above base density must be attainable, provided on-site and restricted for at least 30 years.
  • California: State law links density bonuses to the share and affordability of qualifying housing. Additional stacking bonuses and special provisions for entirely affordable projects can permit increases beyond the standard schedules.
  • Fort Lauderdale, Florida: The city describes an optional affordable-housing payment in lieu starting at $10,000 per unit and increasing 3% annually from policy adoption in 2023. The fee applies to every unit in the development, including affordable and market-rate units. The applicable current fee should be confirmed with the city.
  • Miami-Dade County, Florida: Developers may satisfy applicable workforce-housing requirements through a contribution calculated under the county's adopted formula and payment schedule. Requirements vary with project characteristics and location. The county's historic-preservation tax exemption is a separate incentive.
  • Monroe County and Key West, Florida: ROGO and BPAS regulate new residential development through allocation systems associated with growth management and hurricane-evacuation planning. Available allocations, award periods and eligibility depend on the applicable jurisdiction and current program provisions.

What This Means for the Tool

These examples provide context for evaluating development incentives and public benefits. They do not establish a standard price for an SPB density-pool unit or independently validate this tool's valuation method. Tool results should be considered alongside adopted allocation criteria, documented assumptions and project-specific information.

Sources: Adopted codes, ordinances and official program guidance. Confirm current provisions, eligibility and allocation balances before applying a comparison to a project.
